title: Bézier curves and polygon surfaces
subtitle: How fonts, paths and car bodies are drawn with a handful of control points.

why.title: Curves from control points
why.body: Storing a smooth curve as thousands of tiny lines is wasteful and awkward to edit. A parametric curve is a point Q(t) = (x(t), y(t)) as t runs from 0 to 1, defined by a few control points. A spline joins cubic pieces smoothly. Designers drag control points; the curve follows.

bez.title: Bézier curves
bez.body: A cubic Bézier curve has four control points P₀…P₃ and Q(t) = (1−t)³P₀ + 3t(1−t)²P₁ + 3t²(1−t)P₂ + t³P₃. It starts at P₀ tangent to P₀P₁ and ends at P₃ tangent to P₂P₃, and always lies inside the convex hull of its control points. The de Casteljau construction finds the point at t by repeated linear interpolation: join neighbouring control points, take the point a fraction t along each segment, and repeat until one point remains. At t = 0.5 for P = (0,0), (1,3), (4,3), (5,0) the point is 2.5,2.25, which matches (P₀ + 3P₁ + 3P₂ + P₃)/8 = 2.5,2.25.

spline.title: Splines and continuity
spline.body: Long curves are built from several low-degree pieces. C⁰ continuity: the pieces meet. C¹: same tangent direction and speed at the join. C²: same curvature too. For two Bézier segments to join with C¹ the last two points of one and the first two of the next must be collinear and evenly spaced. B-splines and NURBS give local control and exact circles.

surf.title: Polygon surfaces
surf.body: A 3-D object is stored as a polygon mesh: a vertex table (coordinates), an edge table (vertex pairs) and a polygon table (edges of each face). Each face has a surface normal N = (V₂ − V₁) × (V₃ − V₁), needed for lighting and for deciding which side faces the viewer. Smooth surfaces use Bézier patches, revolution and sweeps.

summary.title: Summary
summary.body:
• Bézier: Q(t) from control points; de Casteljau by repeated interpolation.
  • Joins: C⁰, C¹, C²; meshes = vertex, edge, polygon tables.
